items.longBusinessSummary: Nebius Group N.V., a technology company, engages in building full-stack infrastructure to service the global AI industry in the United States, the United Kingdom, and internationally. It offers Nebius builds full-stack infrastructure for AI, including large-scale GPU clusters, cloud platforms, and tools and services for developers. The company also provides TripleTen, an edtech platform for re-skilling individuals for careers in technolgy; and Avride, which develops autonomous driving technology for self-driving cars and delivery robotics. It has a strategic alliance with NVIDIA Corporation to support the expansion of the company's AI cloud infrastructure. The company was formerly known as Yandex N.V. and changed its name to Nebius Group N.V. in August 2024. Nebius Group N.V. was founded in 1989 and is based in Schiphol, the Netherlands.

Title: Top Investor: CoreWeave Locked In Compute “Way, Way Under Market.” Rising GPU Prices Won’t Save It
Author: Gian Estrada   Sun, November 1, 2026 at 12:49 PM GMT+1 6 min read
Published: 2026-11-01T11:49:09+00:00
=== BODY ===
CoreWeave jumped 7.94% on Oct. 27 after bringing new capacity online in Denmark, and Nebius rose 11.22%. By the Oct. 30 close, CoreWeave had given the gain back at $54.87.
Atreides Management's Gavin Baker says GPU rents rose every day in October, but CoreWeave locked much of its capacity into long contracts that now pay far below market.
CoreWeave pays today's prices to build and borrow: its total debt, including leases, reached $51.6 billion in June, and its 2032 bonds yielded close to 15% in October.
Higher rents mostly help operators with free capacity and cheap funding, so CoreWeave's Nov. 10 report on interest costs and renewals is the next test.
CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) couldn't hold on to its best day in weeks.
The stock jumped 7.94% to $59.57 on Oct. 27 after CoreWeave brought new capacity online at its first data center in Denmark, and fellow neocloud Nebius Group (NBIS:NASDAQ) rose 11.22%. By the Oct. 30 close, CoreWeave was back at $54.87, after Microsoft's capital spending came in below estimates and tech stocks sold off. That capped an October in which CoreWeave's 9.625% notes due 2032 fell below 80 cents on the dollar.
The odd part is that GPUs have rarely been harder to rent. As Gavin Baker, managing partner and CIO of Atreides Management, said on TBPN on Oct. 27:
"October has kind of been a strange month because the price to rent, essentially any kind of a GPU, has gone up every day."
So why isn't CoreWeave cashing in? Baker had an answer for that too. "CoreWeave is great," he said. "They just sadly locked in a vast amount of compute" in long-term contracts "that are now way, way under market."
Committed contracts made up 98% of CoreWeave's 2025 revenue, and the average contract, weighted by size, ran about five years at the end of 2025.
Baker says anyone who signed a long-term compute contract before about May 2026 is "way in the money." CoreWeave sat on the other side of a lot of those deals. And on the second-quarter call in August, CFO Nitin Agrawal said the capacity coming up for renewal is "a very limited part of our fleet."
Its margins aren't rising with the market either. CoreWeave's gross margin peaked at 74.3% in 2024 and slipped to 71.7% in 2025…
…and it fell again this year: cost of revenue took 34.1% of second-quarter revenue, up from 25.8% a year earlier.
See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on CoreWeave, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See CoreWeave's Analyst Ratings
Buying future capacity is just as tight. In Baker's words, "You have to pay a truly vast amount to bring on a cluster in mid to late twenty seven."
That's a problem for a company that builds with borrowed money. CoreWeave's total debt, including leases, went from $2 billion at the end of 2023 to $29.8 billion at the end of 2025…
…and reached $51.6 billion by June 30, $16.5 billion of it lease liabilities.
That money keeps getting more expensive. CoreWeave's dollar bonds went from a 9.00% coupon in July 2025 to 9.75% in April 2026, and October's slide pushed the yield on its 9.625% notes due 2032, sold in June, close to 15%. Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, said on Prof G Markets on Oct. 28: "I think it's prohibitive for them to raise debt at 15% and build AI data centers."
In the second quarter, depreciation and interest together ate 79% of revenue. For the third quarter, management guided to interest expense of $860 million to $940 million, against adjusted operating income of just $200 million to $260 million.
Analysts don't expect profits soon, either. They see a normalized loss of $3.99 a share in 2026 and $1.97 in 2027, then a $1.61 profit in 2028:
A year ago, they expected a $2.23 profit in 2027. Estimates have fallen while rents climbed.
Fixed prices cut both ways. If new supply pushes rents back down, those long contracts will protect CoreWeave's revenue.
CoreWeave is adjusting, too. It raised prices about 25% across its GPU lineup in July, and management says contracts signed in the second quarter carry contribution margins 5 to 10 points above recent ones. Baker added that "CoreWeave is very aware of this. They're trying to get more spot exposure." Not all of its money is expensive, either: a Meta-backed $8.5 billion loan in March priced at about 5.9% fixed.
But higher prices only apply to new capacity, which costs "a truly vast amount" to build and must be financed in today's market. Baker hopes the crunch concentrates supply in "the competent operators where they can finance it through prepayments." That describes Nebius better: about 70% of its second-quarter deals came with prepayments covering 50% to 60% of the capex tied to them.
Rising GPU rents won't fix CoreWeave while it pays this much for money. Its cheapest loans lean on contracts with customers like Meta, and its unsecured bonds yielded 15% or more in October. Until it can borrow on better terms, the shortage mostly helps CoreWeave's customers.
There's one wild card. NVIDIA bought $2 billion of CoreWeave stock at $87.20 a share in January, and Eisman allows that "maybe, you know, NVIDIA will come in and backstop the whole company."
Barring that, CoreWeave's third-quarter report on Nov. 10 will show how far interest expense outruns operating income, and whether any renewals are coming in at today's prices.

Title: Nebius Lost 35% Last Month As Contagion Spikes: One Wall Street Pro Says 165% Gains Are Coming
Author: Alex Sirois   Mon, November 2, 2026 at 4:45 PM GMT+1 6 min read
Published: 2026-11-02T15:45:07+00:00
=== BODY ===
Nebius (NBIS) dropped 35% last month amid neocloud contagion, but Northland analyst Nehal Chokshi raised his target to $410, implying 166% upside.
CoreWeave (CRWV) fell 37% and Applied Digital (APLD) dropped 27%, with analysts projecting 145% and 242% upside respectively from current levels.
Nebius grew Q2 revenue 454% year-over-year with a 41% EBITDA margin, and management confirmed a year-end run-rate target ranging from $7 billion to $9 billion.
Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Nebius Group didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat NBIS. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.
Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) currently trades at $154.14, and the average Wall Street price target is $281. That gap works out to 82.3% upside.
Nebius rents out GPU compute, inference and managed AI services that run on NVIDIA hardware. It sells them through Nebius AI Cloud, which brought in 98% of group revenue last quarter. Wall Street has been paying attention. Deals like a $27B five-year Meta agreement and a $37.5B backlog of remaining performance obligations explain why.
The Street's most bullish analyst sees far more upside than the average. Northland Securities holds the Street-high $410.00 target, which implies about 166% upside. The stock fell more than 30% in a month while consensus implies 82.3% upside, so investors have to decide whether this is an overreaction to contagion or a fair discount for a business that needs enormous amounts of capital.
Nebius shares fell 34.65% over the past month. Nebius released no earnings or contract news to explain the drop. The first blow came from Gartner, which predicted that more than 80% of neocloud providers will stop operating independently by 2030. Gartner cited cost pressure and "a lack of a differentiating business model."
24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.
The report is free, and you can see why we think each stock is a top investment today.
Fear then spread from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV). Investors worried about its debt load after hotter inflation data lifted bets on rate hikes. Microsoft then reported capital spending that fell short of estimates, which sent the group down again. In the latest session alone, Nebius dropped 10.38%, compared with a 1.77% dip for the S&P 500.
Nebius has funding risks of its own. It carries $8.5B of convertible debt at book value. It also sold 12.7 million shares through its at-the-market program at $224. The company expects $20 billion to $25 billion of capex in 2026. Three customers made up 24%, 21%, 14% of second-quarter revenue.
Most analysts are staying put. Of 21 analysts covering the stock, 2 rate it a Strong Buy, 12 a Buy, 5 a Hold, 1 a Sell and 1 a Strong Sell. Northland's Nehal Chokshi raised his target from $248.00 to $410.00 and kept his Outperform rating.
Northland's case has three parts. It expects Nebius to win an oversized share of the market for leasing AI infrastructure as a service. It expects low-cost power to widen margins. And it puts about $29 per share of value to Avride, TripleTen and Toloka.
The operating results back up the growth side of that case. Second-quarter revenue reached $582.3M, up 454% from a year earlier, with a 41% adjusted EBITDA margin. Annualized run-rate revenue hit $3 billion at the end of the quarter. Management confirmed its year-end run-rate target of $7 billion to $9 billion. Deals signed in Q2 brought in $20 million to $25 million per megawatt, and customer prepayments covered 50% to 60% of the related capex. Management said Nebius "could sell today our entire 2027 capacity on these terms if we wanted to."
Executives said the biggest revenue impact from new contracts arrives in 2027, and formal 2027 guidance is due later this year. Price targets are estimates. This one also depends on Nebius reaching its year-end goal of 5 gigawatts of contracted power.
The whole neocloud group sold off together, and analysts see bigger rebounds elsewhere.
CoreWeave fell 37.02% over the past month to $54.87. Its average target is $134.58, which implies 145.3% upside. Most of its 42 analysts are bullish. 31 rate it a Buy or Strong Buy, and Goldman Sachs recently upgraded it to Buy. A debt-to-equity ratio of 8.94 helps explain the steeper discount.
Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD) dropped 26.9% in a month to $17.82. Its average target of $60.94 implies 242% upside. Thirteen of its 15 analysts rate it a Buy or Strong Buy, and none rate it a Sell. Treat that target with caution, since it is above the stock's 52-week high of $50.73.
Applied Digital has the largest implied upside among these stocks, and Nebius has the lowest. That ranking mostly reflects how much better Nebius has held up this year.
At $154.14, Nebius is well below the $281 consensus target from 21 analysts, an implied 82.3% upside. The stock lost 34.65% over the past month, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.91%.
Over the longer term, Nebius is up 84.15% year to date, compared with 10.82% for the S&P 500. Its 52-week range runs from $73.52 to $299.86, and it trades at a forward P/E of 31.
Bulls get more confidence if the 2027 capacity expansion arrives on schedule and pricing holds near the $20 million to $25 million per megawatt it booked in Q2. If that happens, the $37.5B backlog turns into revenue and margin, and $281 comes within reach.
Downside risks grow if Gartner's call on consolidation proves right and supply catches up with demand. In that case pricing slips, convertible securities and at-the-market share sales keep diluting holders, and the heavy reliance on Meta and Microsoft becomes a liability.
Nebius has contracted demand. It has $236 million of quarterly adjusted EBITDA and far less net debt than CoreWeave, so a contagion selloff of more than 30% looks overdone. Still, the $410 target needs everything to go right, so I'd set expectations closer to the consensus.
If you have cash sitting in your account right now, give this two minutes. After more than two decades of helping investors beat the market, our top analysts at 24/7 Wall St. put together a definitive report on the Top 10 Stocks To Buy Today. And NBIS wasn't one of them.
Contact editorial@247wallst.com for any questions or corrections.

Title: Is Nebius Stock a Buy After Its 36% Pullback?
Author: Justin Pope, The Motley Fool   Sun, November 1, 2026 at 8:35 PM GMT+1 5 min read
Published: 2026-11-01T19:35:00+00:00
=== BODY ===
The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has been the driving force behind the stock market's strong performance these past few years. But recent concerns over funding for data centers and other AI infrastructure have sparked a sell-off among AI stocks over the past month.
Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS), an AI cloud company, has been caught in the turmoil. Shares traded near $250 in September, nearly touching $300 per share before the AI trade began to lose steam.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
All of a sudden, Nebius sits 36% off its high. Should investors buy Nebius Group stock? The financing concerns matter because Nebius needs substantial capital to build the AI data centers it leases to AI companies. Here's what you need to know.
Computing power is arguably the most important bottleneck for AI's advancement and adoption. Smarter AI models and more users both translate to higher demand for compute.
Nebius plays an important role in this. The company builds specialized data centers, fitted with Nvidia graphics processing unit (GPU) chips designed specifically for AI workloads. It then leases them to its customers, primarily Microsoft and Meta Platforms.
These two companies are among the largest AI hyperscalers, so their computing needs are setting Nebius on an explosive growth trajectory. Wall Street analysts estimate that revenue growth will continue to accelerate, finishing this year at around $3.34 billion and then soaring to $12.24 billion next year.
Nebius has more than $40 billion in long-term commitments from investment-grade customers, and AI GPU leader Nvidia has a stake in the company. Nebius is also among the first companies to offer access to AI servers using Nvidia's Vera Rubin AI chip platform.
A major issue facing Nebius is that it must build out its AI data centers before it can really monetize them. As a result, the company is burning through startling amounts of capital ahead of this expected revenue surge next year. Management anticipates $20 billion to $25 billion in capital expenditures (capex) this year and is funding them through a combination of debt and new stock.
All that growth has certainly enticed investors, who have driven Nebius' market capitalization to $43 billion. That's arguably a hefty valuation for a company that's basically diluting existing shareholders and loading up its balance sheet with debt before it's consistently profitable.
It's only fair to wonder what the future holds. The industry-wide concerns center on speculation about how much more capital is available in the debt markets for these companies to access as AI spending continues adding up.
Elon Musk recently predicted on X that many AI cloud companies could fail, stating that debt markets have already pulled back on lending to companies without meaningful revenue streams outside of data centers. That said, Nebius may be on solid footing.
Nebius is receiving significant upfront payments from its customers as part of its deals. Management guided for total prepayments of around $9 billion in 2026, helping the company stomach its sky-high capex. Nebius also still had about $8 billion in cash at the end of the second quarter.
There's no clear-cut answer because it's difficult to know what Nebius' margins will ultimately look like. More profitable companies often sustain higher valuations than unprofitable or low-margin businesses.
There's also a risk that hyperscalers will eventually back off their aggressive spending if they cannot monetize AI enough to justify the continued spending.
As of right now, the stock trades at less than four times next year's revenue estimate of $12.24 billion. That's pretty low and may not require unrealistic profit margins to justify it, given the staggering anticipated revenue growth next year.
That makes Nebius a solid buy for risk-seeking growth investors.
